title: Bread and wine (Genesis 14:17–20)
hook: Melchisedech, king and priest, brings out bread and wine; named in the Roman Canon

segments.voice: Yesterday, go forth: Abram at seventy-five, walking with no map. Your line was go, and I will show you. What first step did you take? Day three hundred forty-six.

Some characters in the Bible get whole books. Some get a chapter. This one gets three verses, and then vanishes. Abram has just come back from a night raid. Four kings had carried off his nephew Lot, and Abram chased them north with three hundred eighteen men and brought everyone home. He's tired, dusty, a winner. On the road back, a king comes out to meet him. Not with an army. Not with a bill. With bread, and wine. And then he's gone from the story, and yet his name is still spoken in a prayer at Catholic altars.
screen: `A NIGHT RAID, LOT RESCUED.` → `A KING COMES OUT TO MEET HIM.` → `THREE VERSES, THEN GONE.`

segments.voice: First, who he is. In the Douay-Rheims: "But Melchisedech the king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God." A king and a priest at once. His name in Hebrew means king of righteousness. Salem means peace, and later tradition identifies it with Jerusalem. He has no family tree, no beginning or end in the story. He just appears. Second, what he does. He blesses Abram by the most high God, maker of heaven and earth, and he blesses God for the victory. And Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The man God called to be a blessing is himself blessed by a stranger. Third, where he turns up again. In a psalm, God says to the king, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." And the Letter to the Hebrews takes that line and applies it to Christ: a priest not by birth in Aaron's family, but like Melchisedech, forever. Fourth, why Catholics say his name. In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he once accepted the gifts of Abel, the sacrifice of Abraham, and the offering of the high priest Melchisedech. The Catechism sees in his bread and wine a sign that points ahead to the Eucharist. Readers in other churches, following Hebrews, also see in him a picture of Christ's priesthood, and draw the link to the altar differently or not at all. Either way, the shape is the same: a priest, a blessing, bread and wine, long ago.
screen: `A KING AND A PRIEST AT ONCE.` · `ABRAM IS BLESSED AND GIVES A TENTH.` · `A PRIEST FOREVER, IN THE PSALM.` · `NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.` · then, large: `BRINGING FORTH BREAD AND WINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice bread and wine as signs. If there's bread, or a cracker, or any food nearby, put it in front of you. If not, picture a loaf on a table. Settle, and breathe. Think about how much it took to get here: wheat in a field, rain, someone's hands at harvest, an oven, a truck. Grapes on a vine, crushed and waited on. Ordinary things that took a long time and many people. Let that sink in. If you pray, you can give thanks for the food in front of you and for the people who brought it to you. The bell holds the time.
Bread and wine. What Melchisedech, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, brought out to bless Abram. Catholics see in it a sign of the Eucharist.
Your line: bread and wine, long ago. Today, at one meal, take the first bite slowly and remember how far it came to reach you. Day three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: In the Roman Canon, the priest asks God to accept the Mass's offering as he accepted the offering of Melchisedech, and Genesis 14:18–20 is read on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in one year of the cycle.

fork.setup: you're a king and a priest. Abram is on the road home from rescuing Lot, tired and dusty. how do you meet him?
options: with an army, to claim a share of the spoils.
with bread and wine, and a blessing.
with a demand that he pay tribute.
fork.reveal: Melchisedech brings forth bread and wine and blesses Abram by the most high God. Abram gives him a tenth.

original.note: Hebrew: Melchizedek, king of righteousness. Douay-Rheims spells it Melchisedech.

trapdoor: what you thought: a minor king in a war story.
what it means: a priest-king who blesses Abram with bread and wine, remembered as a sign of Christ's priesthood.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 14, Psalm 109 (110 in Hebrew numbering), Hebrews 7, and the Roman Canon all name him.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 14:18 and Psalm 109:4 quoted from memory; the Douay-Rheims 14:18 ends with a comma before verse 19. Confirm.
Salem = peace, and identified with Jerusalem by later tradition (Psalm 75:3 DR / 76:2). Confirm.
'Centuries later, in a psalm': rough dating of Psalm 110 relative to the Abraham narrative; consider softening to 'centuries later'.
'Many Protestant readers see in him a picture of Christ's priesthood, without the link to the altar': confirm this is fair and unranked.
howItsDone: Genesis 14:18–20 is the first reading for Corpus Christi, Year C; confirm. CCC 1333 (Melchizedek's offering prefigures the Church's), CCC 1544.

Editor review (days 333-350): cut the undated 'centuries later', the superlative 'the oldest Eucharistic Prayer' (now 'the first', its numbering) and 'many Protestant readers'. The meanings 'king of righteousness' and Salem = peace rest on Hebrews 7:2, already cited.
